transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Could you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I suppose what finally pushed me to come in is my concentration has gotten… unreliable. I’m a dentist, so I’ll be at the clinic reviewing a chart, and I’ll realize I’ve read the same line three times and still haven’t taken it in. Or at home I do watercolor sometimes—nothing grand, just washes mostly—and I’ll be laying one out and suddenly my mind is off chasing everything that could go wrong. It’s frustrating, honestly, because I’ve always been pretty careful and focused.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about things, even when there isn't a clear reason, and does it feel hard to control those worries?

Yes… yes, I do. I mean, I try to talk myself down, the way I would with a nervous patient in the chair—calm, practical, one step at a time. But it doesn’t really stay put. One concern turns into another, and then suddenly I’m checking emails again, or going back over my notes, or asking the same question twice when I probably already know the answer.

It’s not always that there’s a real reason right in front of me. It just… keeps moving along on its own, if that makes sense.
Has this kind of worrying been happening to you almost every day for at least six months, even when things seem to be going fine?

Yes, I think so. It really started when I began the formal retirement process… that was about a year and three months ago now. Funny, I thought starting that process would feel like relief, you know, after all these years looking into people’s mouths all day—but instead it sort of opened this door in my head and the worrying just kept coming through. So yes, more than six months.
Do you notice any physical symptoms like restlessness, fatigue, muscle tension, or trouble sleeping when you’re feeling this way?

Yes, fatigue, definitely. By midafternoon I feel sort of… wrung out, I suppose. Not just “I could use a coffee” tired—more like even if I had a quiet morning, or tried to rest a bit, it doesn’t really reset me.

It’s strange because I used to come home and still have enough in me to pull weeds in the garden or stand at the easel for a while. Now those things feel heavier than they ought to. And then I start thinking about how behind the garden’s getting—well, that’s not really what you asked, sorry. But yes, the tiredness is there.
Do you find it hard to relax, or do you feel tense or restless, especially when you’re not focused on a specific task?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I do better when I’ve got something in front of me—something practical, like a crown prep or even just sorting through instruments, though I’m not doing as much of that now. When there’s a task, my hands know what to do.

But when I’m just sitting… I don’t know if I’d call it tense or restless exactly. Relaxing has never been my great talent. Even on vacations I was the one checking the map, making sure we’d left enough time to get to dinner—my wife used to tease me about that. So it’s hard for me to tell what’s “symptom” and what’s just me being me.
Have you noticed yourself becoming more irritable or easily annoyed, even over small things?

I don’t know that I’d say irritable, exactly. I mean, everyone gets annoyed now and then—if someone leaves the operatory light angled wrong, or, well, I suppose I’m not really in the office the same way anymore.

My wife might have a different answer, honestly. She notices things before I do. But I haven’t really noticed myself snapping over tiny things in a way that stands out to me. I’ve probably been more preoccupied than anything.
Would you say your worrying happens even when there’s no immediate stressor or task to focus on, and does it often feel like your mind is working against you?

Yes… I think that’s fair to say. It can happen when there isn’t anything right in front of me to solve, which is almost worse, because then my mind starts making a list on its own.

I try to talk myself down the way I would with a nervous patient in the chair—calm, logical, one thing at a time. But it doesn’t always work. One concern leads to another, and then I’m checking emails again, or going back over notes, or asking the same question I already asked because I can’t quite leave it alone.

And then, of course, I tell myself I’m just being thorough. Dentists are trained to be thorough—if you’re not, people notice. But lately it feels less like being careful and more like my mind won’t let the matter rest.
Have you had trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, even when you’re tired?

Yes… most nights, I’d say. I’ll be tired—properly tired—and I get into bed thinking I should just drop off. But then the house gets quiet, and that’s when my mind starts going.

I start replaying things like patient transfers, whether I handled some detail properly, money pieces, paperwork… and then somehow I’m thinking about something my accountant said three years ago, or a patient I had back when I first bought the practice. Not that that’s relevant, really.

And even when I do sleep, I’m often awake at four or five, just lying there. It doesn’t feel like I’ve really settled, if that makes sense. Like I slept, but not in a way that did me much good.
Would you say that your worrying is about a variety of different things, not just one specific issue, and that it happens even when there isn't a clear or immediate reason to be concerned?

Yes, I think it’s not just one thing. I wish it were, actually, because then I could put it in a file somewhere and deal with it properly.

It sort of moves around. I’ll worry whether my old patients are being looked after the way I would have looked after them, and then it shifts to whether the practice handoff was financially sensible, and then I’m thinking, well, what am I going to be when I’m fully retired? Just someone in the way, you know?

And sometimes there isn’t a clear reason for it right then. I’ll be making coffee or reading the paper, and suddenly my mind is circling back over all of it. Even I can tell it’s out of proportion sometimes, but knowing that doesn’t seem to stop it.
Do you feel like you're actively struggling to keep your worries under control, even when you know they might not make sense?

Yes, I do. I mean, I can see—at least part of me can see—that some of it isn’t terribly rational. I’ll try to talk to myself the way I’d talk to a nervous patient, you know, calm voice, facts, “let’s not get ahead of ourselves.”

But then it doesn’t stay there. One worry sort of opens the door to the next one, and before I know it I’m checking emails again, or looking back over notes I’ve already gone over, or asking someone the same question because I can’t quite let it sit.

It’s frustrating, really. I used to think of that as being conscientious. In dentistry you don’t exactly get rewarded for missing details. But this feels different—it feels like I’m arguing with my own head and losing.
